name: Supporting the Adults Who Support Students
title: Supporting the Adults Who Support Students
answer: This idea is about using AI to support the adults around special education students, especially paraprofessionals and new teachers, while keeping human review in place. It matters because the people who work most closely with students often get the least training, and paperwork drives burnout. The book's answer is to use AI for short guides, drafts, data organization, and meeting preparation, then return saved time to staff as relief.

sections.body: Special education relies on teachers, paraprofessionals, therapists, and aides. Paraprofessionals may spend the most time with students yet receive the least training. AI can draft brief, clear guides about a student's supports, including how to prompt during a task or respond when a student becomes upset. The case manager checks each guide before anyone shares it. New special education teachers also face a steep learning curve, and AI can help them draft materials, organize data, and prepare for meetings so they have more time to learn from experienced colleagues.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a school or classroom, a case manager or lead teacher can ask an AI tool to turn a student's support plan into a short guide for paraprofessionals. The guide might explain how to prompt a student during a task or how to respond when a student becomes upset, and the case manager reviews it before sharing. For new special education teachers, AI can help draft materials, organize data, and prepare for meetings. A mentor then reviews those AI drafts with the new teacher and explains what to change and why. The text does not give separate grade bands, so these steps apply across special education settings.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text gives no study, figure, or formal evidence label for this idea. It describes a practical approach drawn from the daily realities of special education staffing, training, and paperwork. The claims about paraprofessionals receiving the least training, new teachers facing a steep learning curve, and burnout being a serious problem are presented as practice-based concerns rather than research findings. This idea therefore rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The case manager must review each guide before it is shared, so the decision about what goes to staff stays with a person. A mentor should review AI drafts with a new teacher and explain what to change and why, which keeps judgment and learning with experienced colleagues. If AI reduces paperwork, some of that saved time should go back to staff as relief rather than into more paperwork. Districts can track how much time AI saves and ask staff how they are using it. A tool that saves time but leaves staff just as exhausted has not solved the problem.
